item.title: I will never forget you -- An American elder's cross-Pacific nostalgia for China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13
* At 18, David bid farewell to Huangyuan with his family on a drizzly day. Thinking it was merely a short trip, they left their furniture and bedding sealed in the old house as they were -- no one imagined the farewell would stretch to 38 years. * David spent his childhood and adolescence in Huangyuan. More than three decades later, he returned to his "hometown" over 20 times, doing everything in his power to help the local people and leaving behind one touching story after another. * "For two generations, my family has had a deep love for the Chinese people. This love has lasted for more than 100 years, from my father and mother to me. We love the people of China just as we love our own family." by Xinhua writers Wang Jinjin, Xie Tongqiang, Jiang Yi XINING, China, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- "Have you had dinner yet?" White-haired David Plymire spoke in fluent Huangyuan dialect, leaning toward the webcam in his living room in Springfield, Missouri. His greetings traveled across the Pacific, reaching Tongkhor Ancient Town in Huangyuan County, northwest China's Qinghai Province. "Yes, we have! We're waiting to see you on video!" David's longtime friend Wang Shikang replied from in front of the screen, eager to catch a glimpse of their old friend on the other end of the video call. David spent his childhood and adolescence in Huangyuan. More than three decades later, he returned to his "hometown" over 20 times, doing everything in his power to help the local people and leaving behind one touching story after another. CENTURY-OLD FRIENDSHIP In the 1920s, David's father, Victor Plymire, arrived in Tongkhor town along the ancient Tea Horse Road. In 1932, one-year-old David was brought to the small plateau town, where he spent the next 17 years growing up and came to regard it as his hometown. Time has taken its toll. The trans-Pacific journey has become too physically demanding for David over the past decade. "We all miss you! Almost ten years have passed since you were last able to come to Huangyuan. People here, young and old, miss you," Wang said, waving at him through the screen. Wang told David that they were making the video call from the ancient town's old streets, where many historic buildings had been restored with the help of photographs taken decades earlier by his father, Victor. A century ago, Victor took his camera around Tongkhor, documenting its streets, scenery and residents and leaving behind a unique visual record of life on the plateau. The photographs were later compiled into an album titled Imprint of a Legacy. Dong Baoming, general manager of Huangyuan Dancheng Tourism Development Co., Ltd., said Victor and David's photographs had helped bring the town's past back to life. The images now fill the Imprints exhibition hall, which has opened to the public, offering visitors a glimpse of Huangyuan as it once was. At 18, David bid farewell to Huangyuan with his family on a drizzly day. Thinking it was merely a short trip, they left their furniture and bedding sealed in the old house as they were -- no one imagined the farewell would stretch to 38 years. One moment during the call was particularly poignant. Bai Qiming, son of Bai Yongsheng, David's childhood friend known locally as "Ga Liang-ge," sent his greetings to David through the screen and spoke of how they had missed each other over the years. David fell silent for several seconds before quietly saying, "I can't come back now." TRANS-PACIFIC MEMORIES "Has the weather turned cold there?" David asked, then went on reminiscing about swimming in the town's river in summer and skating on the ice in winter when he was a boy. Memories came flooding back as David recalled how arduous travel had once been. A journey from Huangyuan to Xining took an entire day, with a stop at Zhamalong along the way for a bowl of noodles. "Do you have suanjiujiu (sea buckthorn)? Could you send me some suanjiujiu juice?" David asked with a childlike smile. Wang jokingly reminded David that he had sent him 3 kg of tsampa 15 years ago. David said he had carefully kept the package in his refrigerator ever since. He then recalled hand-grabbed mutton, pickled cabbage and Laba porridge. His longing for the familiar flavors of home and the warmth of everyday life back in Huangyuan went far beyond what the screen could convey. During the video call, David watched a prerecorded video of greetings from Huangyuan residents. Leaning back in his chair, he listened and watched attentively, looking closely at the familiar faces on the screen, sometimes breaking into hearty laughter. "My body is here, but my heart is in Huangyuan. I wish everyone back home peace and happiness," David said. As the conversation turned to shehuo, traditional festive performances held around the Chinese New Year, David spontaneously recited a children's rhyme from Huangyuan that he had known since boyhood: "On the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, the temple gates swing open; village women come to light incense." ENDURING DEVOTION TO HOMETOWN David's correspondence with Wang, then director of Huangyuan County People's Hospital, is preserved in the hospital's history exhibition hall. Several letters reveal a recurring subject: a CT scanner. In their early letters, the two addressed each other formally as "Director Wang" and "Mr. Plymire," discussing practical matters such as customs clearance. But with each of David's return visits to his hometown, the formality gradually melted away, giving rise to the warmer, more familiar terms "old friend" and "brother." Between 1997 and 1999, David made three trips to bring the CT scanner to Huangyuan. When the hospital could not afford the 500,000 yuan (75,000 U.S. dollars) tax bill, he rallied support to cover every penny. The scanner enabled the hospital's first brain surgery and helped save countless lives over its 15 years of service. Today, it rests in the hospital's history exhibition hall, alongside archival records documenting his many other contributions. "Mr. Plymire did more than simply donate a few pieces of equipment. He brought us a powerful source of inspiration," said Huang Jiong, director of Huangyuan County People's Hospital, visibly moved. He noted that David has tirelessly raised funds and mobilized support over the past three decades, helping secure donations of more than 30 pieces of medical equipment, worth a total of 6 million yuan (900,000 dollars). "My hometown has become part of who I am. My flesh and bones are the flesh and bones of Huangyuan," David said during the video call. Speaking about people-to-people exchanges between China and the United States, David slowly switched to English: "For two generations, my family has had a deep love for the Chinese people. This love has lasted for more than 100 years, from my father and mother to me. We love the people of China just as we love our own family." "Although I can no longer come back to visit because I am too old to travel by plane, I remember everyone. In my memories, I still walk along those streets, travel through the countryside, stand beside the rivers and talk with my friends," he said. "I shall always remember you in this life, and I will never forget you in the next." (Video reporters: Jiang Yi, Xie Tongqiang, Xie E, Zhao Yuhe, Zhang Long, Li Zhanyi; video editors: Yang Zeyi, Li Qin, Hui Peipei) ■

item.title: High-frequency data show improving trend in Chinese economy in October
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13
BEIJING, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese economy maintained its steady and improving trend in October, with new growth drivers gaining momentum, official high-frequency data on consumption, trade and investment showed Friday. Big data on offline consumption showed that consumption-related payments increased 2.6 percent year on year in October, according to the State Information Center under the National Development and Reform Commission. Benefits from various consumption-boosting policies continued to materialize, supporting the consumer market's steady growth, according to Geng Dewei, an associate researcher at the center's big data development department. "Service consumption in clothing, food, housing, transportation and tourism has improved simultaneously, and diverse consumption scenarios have been continuously activated," Geng said. The data also showed that the departure deadweight tonnage of cargo ships at major Chinese ports increased 59.1 percent year on year in October, with the growth rate 5.9 percentage points higher than that in September. On the investment front, the contract value of winning bids for new infrastructure projects related to computing power and data increased 45.4 percent year on year, while capital investment in frontier fields such as artificial intelligence and humanoid robots soared 307.4 percent. Geng said the effects of policies to stabilize investment are gradually emerging, with allocated funds being translated into physical progress and the investment structure being optimized. A State Council executive meeting held last week urged faster progress on the construction and implementation of major projects and the country's "six networks" of infrastructure, covering water, power, computing, communications, urban underground pipelines and logistics networks. It called for strengthening confidence and stepping up policy implementation to ensure China meets its major economic and social development targets for the year. China has targeted 2026 growth at 4.5 to 5 percent and will strive for even better results in practice. China's gross domestic product grew 4.5 percent year on year in the third quarter of 2026, higher than the second quarter's reading of 4.3 percent. ■

item.title: China says acts of Japanese right-wing forces blatantly challenge postwar int'l order
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13
BEIJING, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of National Defense said on Friday that acts by Japanese right-wing forces were clearly challenging the postwar international order, after reports that Japan planned to keep labeling China as its greatest strategic challenge and to consider easing restrictions on nuclear weapons. Ministry spokesperson Chen Xi said Japan, as a defeated country in World War II, should have reflected on its history of aggression and war crimes, and drawn lessons from history. "Instead, right-wing forces in Japan keep fabricating false narratives on the so-called China threat, and distorting facts to portray Japan as a victim," Chen said. He said Japan was ramping up defense expenditure, strengthening offensive and long-range strike capabilities, and, worse still, seeking to progressively ease nuclear restrictions. "With such moves, they have not only betrayed Japan's commitment to peace, but also blatantly challenged the postwar international order and the authority of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons," he said. Chen called on the international community to stay highly vigilant and take countermeasures against Japan's push for remilitarization, uphold the international nuclear non-proliferation regime, and defend the security and peace of the world. The remarks came after reports that Japan would continue to label China as its greatest strategic challenge in its revised three security documents, and increase its defense spending to around 70 to 80 trillion yen (about 438 to 500 billion U.S. dollars) over the next five years. The Japanese government was also said to be considering amending its National Security Strategy to include exceptions to the three non-nuclear principles, which potentially allows the transport of nuclear weapons into Japan in emergencies. ■

item.title: Explainer: How the CPC confines power to institutional cage
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13
BEIJING, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- The Communist Party of China (CPC) has mapped out institutional arrangements to keep the power of officials in check and advance its fight against graft and misuse of power in a systematic manner. The CPC, founded in 1921, has clearly defined in national laws the legal boundaries of what officials can and cannot do. In addition, the Party had over 3,000 regulations in force as of 2025, forming a robust institutional framework to regulate the exercise of power. The eight-point decision on improving official conduct sets clear rules for officials' work practices, including research trips, meetings and documentation, while curbing extravagance and abuse of privileges. In late October, a resolution on persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance, adopted at the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee, outlined further measures to strengthen checks on and oversight over the exercise of power. The resolution called for improving relevant institutions and mechanisms to ensure that the delegation, exercise and oversight of power are better coordinated, with powers and responsibilities clearly defined, procedures transparent and records traceable. It proposed to strengthen ongoing monitoring of corruption-related risks and hidden dangers and establish mechanisms for coordinating early warning of and punishment for corruption. Since 2012, the anti-corruption storm has swept every corner of public office, netting both high-ranking "tigers" and lower-level "flies." Over the years, discipline inspection and supervisory organs nationwide have filed over 8 million cases and punished nearly 8 million people, including 963 officials registered with and supervised by the CPC Central Committee. One key factor behind the achievements has been the effort to put power in an institutional cage, including the establishment of a nationwide supervisory system to bring everyone in public office, regardless of Party membership, under supervision. The resolution underscored efforts to improve the Party and state supervision system and refine inspection methods. The inspection system, a key instrument of intra-Party oversight, allows higher-level Party authorities to send teams to examine how officials exercise power and carry out the central leadership's policies. Inspectors interview officials and members of the public, review documents and receive complaints. They report their findings to Party authorities. Innovating inspection methods could involve better coordination of different forms of inspection, the use of a wider range of oversight tools, and the application of new technologies. In recent years, by integrating data from multiple government departments and using big data analytics to identify anomalies and trace hidden connections, disciplinary and supervisory authorities have been able to uncover cases involving misappropriation of public funds, fraudulent claims for government subsidies and the abuse of public office for private gain. A system is only as strong as its implementation. The resolution emphasized the need to enhance the binding force of institutions and ensure that all are equal before institutions. ■

item.title: Xi stresses persevering with full, rigorous Party self-governance in state-owned enterprises
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13
BEIJING, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has emphasized the need to persevere with full and rigorous Party self-governance in state-owned enterprises (SOEs) to provide strong guarantees for SOEs and state capital to get stronger, do better, and grow bigger. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a recent instruction on Party building in SOEs. He noted that Party building in SOEs has been strengthened and new progress has been made across the board since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012. Xi urged further efforts to uphold and strengthen the Party's overall leadership of SOEs, better integrate the Party's leadership into all links of corporate governance, advance in-depth integration of Party building with production and operation, foster high-caliber, professional teams, and build good conduct, enforce discipline and fight corruption. Cai Qi, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and a member of the CPC Central Committee Secretariat, speaks at a meeting on Party building in state-owned enterprises (SOEs) in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 13, 2026. An important instruction by Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, was conveyed at the meeting held in Beijing on Friday. (Xinhua/Yue Yuewei) The instruction was conveyed at a meeting on Party building in SOEs held in Beijing on Friday. Cai Qi, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and a member of the Secretariat of the CPC Central Committee, attended the event. Cai said Xi's important instruction has charted the course for further strengthening Party building in SOEs. Cai emphasized the need to accurately grasp the new requirements for Party building in SOEs arising from the evolving global, national and Party conditions. He called for efforts to resolutely combat corruption and further institutionalize and standardize the Party's leadership over SOEs. ■

item.title: Xi to attend APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, related events in Shenzhen
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13
BEIJING, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping will chair the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting and deliver remarks, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson announced Friday. The meeting will be held in Shenzhen from Nov. 18 to 19 under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," the spokesperson said. The APEC CEO Summit will be held in Shenzhen from Nov. 17 to 18 under the theme "To Prosper and Win the Future Together," the spokesperson said, adding that President Xi will attend the opening ceremony and deliver a keynote speech. President Xi will hold a welcome banquet for participating leaders and representatives, and hold bilateral meetings with foreign leaders on the sidelines of the meeting, the spokesperson added. ■
